title: Founder of Edinburgh's First Coffee Shop Issues Challenge to the UK Government: Give us twelve months to show that there is a solution... A Brilliantly Practical Suggestion.

content_html_sanitized:
Posted June 3, 2002
(MarijuanaNews note: My friend Kevin Williamson intends to open a Dutch-style cannabis coffee shop in the Scottish capital very soon.
See

Because of his prominence in Edinburgh literary circles, I have always thought that Kevin is the ideal person to be doing this, Prince William being otherwise busy.

Kevin has now issued a challenge to the UK government that is perfectly timed and directly targeted at the absurdity of the new regulations, which will see cannabis reclassified this summer, but not allow legal sales.

He is urging that the government try the coffee shop system for a year and find out what happens.

Kevin says, " As it will stand the new law is a halfway house - albeit a welcome one. Users will no longer be arrested but will still be sent to the black market to buy it. The logic in that is non existent. "

That absurdity is the result of the Parliamentary committee report that not only failed to examine the Dutch experience, but actually misrepresented it saying that " The Netherlands' policy on cannabis is, in effect, toleration of personal use. "

Of course, the foundation of all Dutch drugs policies is the separation of the cannabis market from hard drugs by tolerating the sale of cannabis, not just " personal use. " In any case, lying about the very nature of the Dutch experience makes it rather difficult to learn from it. So that is where Kevin's challenge comes in.

This is actually a very practical proposal. The prohibitionists strenuously ignoring the Dutch experience like to claim that it would be too great a risk to legalize cannabis. And then there are the treaties, etc., etc.,

Well, this gets around both objections. If it doesn't work, if at the end of the year the sky has fallen, then it would be easy to close the shops, easier in fact than if the shops are all operating in a " grey area. "

Obviously, such a one-year test would be a way for other Commonwealth countries especially Canada and New Zealand -- to find their way to more sensible policies.

This is a practical example of what I meant by " freedom has nothing to fear from the truth. " Of course, the non-stop lying from the prohibitionists that will accompany such a move will be a problem...

Freedom? Try you'll like it!)

From Kevin Williamson:


REBEL INC NEWSLETTER #2 - EDINBURGH'S CANNABIS COFFEESHOP CHALLENGE

Our challenge to the UK Government:

The UK government has finally bitten the bullet and begun the process of changing the mess that has been called Drugs Policy.

The Home Office Select Committee report - which is finally on the desk of Home Secretary David Blunkett - has advised reclassifying cannabis from a Class B to a Class C drug.

As it will stand the new law is a halfway house - albeit a welcome one. Users will no longer be arrested but will still be sent to the black market to buy it. The logic in that is non existent.

To help the politicians out of their predicament those of us involved with the proposed Rebel Inc cannabis coffeeshop in Edinburgh want to issue this genuine challenge....

Give us twelve months to show that there is a solution...

Cannabis Coffeeshop Challenge

So it is hard to imagine how things might get worse.

From the UK government's perspective, taking this challenge could offer some benefits beyond the learning opportunity. If they made tolerance of the shops conditional on their meeting certain standards as do the Dutch then they will have greater influence over events than they will if they just ignore them and/or sporadically harass them, as is the current policy.

In addition to having an absolute ban on hard drugs in the coffee shops, the Dutch sharply restrict advertising, too much in fact. The age limit is 18, which is too high. And there is the obvious requirement that the shops not create a public nuisance.

The UK government could offer tolerance for a year for shops that comply with similar regulations.

The biggest problem with coming up with such regulations is that the UK government will either have to acknowledge the existence of the Dutch model, or they will have to talk to people who have some knowledge of cannabis, and they seem to be very reluctant to do either of these things.)

Our pledge would be to provide a DETAILED REPORT on the experiment and, after 12 months, appear before any government committee at Westminster or Holyrood to answer questions on the experiment. We would also extend to any politicians, anti-drug campaigners, or law enforcement agencies, an open invitation to visit the premises - at any time they wish - in order to see for themselves how it could work in practice.

There are other cannabis coffeeshops already open or planned too so the experiment needn't be confined to just Edinburgh.

The benefit to the government - and the public - would be that they could get all the necessary information needed BEFORE taking such an important and far-reaching step.

If, at the end of the twelve months, the experiment is deemed a failure by general consensus then we'd close it down. In other words a potential solution - to the grey area about to arise in cannabis law - is about to be put in front of the authorities.

The only other alternative on offer is to continue sending cannabis users back to the criminals operating in the black market in order to buy cannabis.

We believe our proposed experiment is a more adult and socially desirable response to a very real problem that won't go away.

So the challenge is now made. Hopefully the challenge will be accepted and the problems associated with all drug use can be dealt with more effectively than to date.

NB The opening date and location of the coffeeshop will be revealed EXCLUSIVELY through the Rebel Inc Newsletter so if you ain't subscribed yet then click along to the official website ... or spread the word by forwarding this!

From all at Rebel Inc HQ:
Peace, Love, and, as always, FTM
